title: India Orders GitHub to Take Down Jack Dorsey's Bitchat Amid Protest Crackdown
excerpt: The Indian government directed GitHub to remove repositories for the Bluetooth mesh messaging app within three hours, citing law enforcement concerns as students at Delhi's Jantar Mantar turned to offline communication tools during internet shutdowns.
body:
• India's I4C ordered GitHub to remove three Bitchat repositories within three hours, invoking Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act after students at Jantar Mantar began using the Bluetooth mesh app during internet shutdowns.
  • Bitchat, an open-source project founded by former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey in 2025, enables peer-to-peer messaging without internet, servers, or user registration — capabilities the government says hamper lawful interception.
  • The order also invokes criminal conspiracy and national unity provisions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, signalling the government views offline communication tools as a security threat during civil unrest.
  • GitHub has complied with the order and taken down the repositories, though the open-source code may already be mirrored elsewhere.

India's cybercrime agency ordered GitHub to remove the source code and Android releases of Bitchat, a Bluetooth mesh messaging app built by former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey, as the government escalated its crackdown on communication channels used by student protesters in New Delhi.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), which operates under the Union Home Ministry, issued the takedown notice late on July 23, directing GitHub to remove or disable access to three URLs — the main Bitchat repository, its Android repository, and the Android releases page — within three hours, according to Inc42 and MediaNama, which reviewed the order.

Dorsey shared the I4C notice on X, writing: "The government of India does not like technologies like bitchat and wants it taken down." GitHub has complied with the order, according to MediaNama.

"The government of India does not like technologies like bitchat and wants it taken down."

— Jack Dorsey, former Twitter CEO and Bitchat developer

Why the Government Targeted Bitchat

The I4C notice laid out a sweeping rationale for the takedown. It stated that Bitchat enables anonymous communication over Bluetooth mesh networks without mandatory registration, phone number verification, or centralised logging — features that "significantly" impede lawful interception and investigation by law enforcement.

https://x.com/coinbureau/status/2080621242810548397

The order warned that such platforms could be exploited to evade surveillance, bypass internet shutdowns, coordinate unlawful assemblies, spread misinformation, and facilitate "radicalisation and criminal conspiracies." It also noted the absence of a central service provider limits agencies' ability to obtain subscriber information or communication records.

Beyond the IT Act's safe harbour provisions, the notice invoked Section 43 of the IT Act for unauthorised computer access, along with Sections 84B and 84C for abetting such offences. It also cited the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — specifically Section 61 on criminal conspiracy and Sections 196 and 197 dealing with promoting enmity between groups and statements harmful to national unity, according to MediaNama.

The NEET Protest Backdrop

The takedown came amid an intensifying standoff between the Modi government and student protesters demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in the NEET-UG 2026 exam. The exam, originally held on May 3, was cancelled on May 12 after paper leak allegations, re-conducted on June 21, with results declared on July 16.

Protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — joined by climate activist Sonam Wangchuk, who has been on a hunger strike for over 20 days — have centred at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi. On July 20, tens of thousands attempted to march to Parliament and were met with tear gas and baton charges; about 150 protesters were hospitalised, according to Reuters and CNN.

On July 23, the Home Ministry ordered the suspension of mobile internet services within a 1.5-km radius of Jantar Mantar from 4 p.m. to midnight under the Telecommunications Act, 2023. The shutdown extended to a second day, disrupting digital payments and forcing businesses in the Connaught Place commercial district to close early, Reuters reported. Sixteen metro stations were also shuttered.

It was in this communications blackout that protesters turned to offline mesh networking tools like Bitchat — which is precisely what prompted the government's order targeting the app's source code on GitHub.

Broader Crackdown on Digital Tools

The Bitchat takedown fits into a wider pattern of the government tightening control over digital platforms. The I4C has issued at least 426 content takedown notices since March 2024, according to government submissions in the X (formerly Twitter) case before the Karnataka High Court. Earlier this year, MeitY proposed amendments to the IT Rules that would make government advisories legally binding on intermediaries and require content removal within three hours of a government notice.

Delhi Police have also deployed CCTV vans with facial recognition technology at the Jantar Mantar protest site, according to MediaNama, while Meta blocked an Instagram reel by Maktoob Hindi covering the protests.

What's Next

As an open-source project, Bitchat's code is likely mirrored across multiple platforms and developer machines, making a complete suppression difficult. The episode is expected to fuel a growing debate about the government's use of Section 79(3)(b) takedowns — a legal mechanism originally designed for content moderation — to target source code and software tools.

MediaNama has scheduled an online briefing on July 28 to examine internet shutdowns, Bitchat, facial recognition, and protest surveillance. Nationwide demonstrations have been called for Friday, with protests spreading beyond Delhi to Ranchi, Pune, Thiruvananthapuram, and Kolkata.
nri_angle: The takedown of an open-source communication tool built by a prominent US tech founder raises questions about digital rights and censorship that resonate with diaspora Indians who rely on open platforms to stay connected with developments in India.
author: Diaspora Desk
